content.text: Initial research suggests that the 1986 Efron paper directly addresses the core issue of biased error rates when evaluating a model on the same data it was trained on. Considering this, further investigation will focus on the related works, including the 2004 Efron paper and others, to gain a more comprehensive understanding.

Examining related works, Wolpert (1992) highlights overfitting with in-sample predictions and the need for cross-validation.  Stone (1974) and Geisser (1975) present early work on cross-validation and predictive sample reuse. Breiman (1996) explores out-of-bag estimation and stacked regressions.

Considering Fisher/Mallows (1973), in-sample fit is distinct from expected prediction error. Hastie et al. (2001/2009) in "Elements of Statistical Learning" detail model assessment and selection with emphasis on out-of-sample error and optimism. Other works of note are Bien/Tibshirani, Chernozhukov (2018) which focus on residual estimation and Guo et al. (2017) discuss calibration of neural networks.

The mean residual correction ensures zero error on the *same* data used for its calculation, but this doesn't validate performance on unseen data. The core issue centers on whether the correction generalizes beyond the initial, finite sample. This specific scenario is relevant for assessing whether a fixed offset is removed.

The literature consistently indicates a key pitfall: evaluating a model or correction on the same data used for its derivation leads to overly optimistic performance estimates that do not generalize. In-sample error metrics systematically underestimate true prediction error, due to the model's overfitting to the training data. Cross-validation or held-out sets are essential to obtain a realistic assessment of predictive validity and avoid degenerate learning.

The cited literature consistently reinforces that post-hoc corrections calibrated on the same data as the original model will produce overoptimistic error estimates. Cross-validation or held-out datasets are necessary to get a realistic assessment of the correction's generalization. This addresses the problem of whether a scalar offset is a reliable measure of model performance.
